title: Ghosts, vampires and witches are anything but scary to Louisiana's tourism boosters
excerpt: “It’s fashionable for hip French Quarter people to complain about ghost tours. But that would be like moving to Aspen, Colorado and complaining about skiing."
content:
Morgan Black used to be a social worker in Los Angeles.

Then, in 2024, during one of her frequent visits to New Orleans, she had an epiphany that led her to change careers and switch hometowns all at once.

"I was walking around the French Quarter and heard several people complain about their boring walking tours," Black said. "Later, I went on Indeed.com and saw an ad for a paranormal tour guide and I said to myself, 'I can rock this.'"

Shortly after, Black moved to New Orleans and began dressing as the "French Quarter Nun" five days a week to lead tours about ghosts, vampires, voodoo and other more esoteric topics.

"People love the spiritual and paranormal, and I love to entertain," Black said. 

She's not the only one.

For three decades, tourists interested in the paranormal have made pilgrimages to New Orleans — often billed as one of the country's most haunted cities — to immerse themselves in the atmosphere.

Every day in the city's oldest neighborhood, scores of guides regale visitors with oft-told stories that range from the tragic fire at Lalaurie Mansion to the legend of a ghostly priest wandering Père Antoine's Alley to a table permanently set for the ghost of a former property owner at Muriel's Jackson Square restaurant.

Tour companies with names like Haunted History or French Quarter Phantoms — and even, incongruously, Lizzie Borden Ghost Tours — fight for consumers' attention online, often sharing a third of the revenues from their tickets, which start around $30, with third-party sales platforms.

There's no economic impact report for Louisiana's haunted tourism industry, which is concentrated in New Orleans and has outposts in St. Francisville, Baton Rouge, the River Parishes and other spots, but the region is widely recognized as a domestic hub that contributes to the $34 billion global "dark tourism" sector, a much larger category that also includes travel to battlefields and the sites of disasters and infamous crimes.

Activity revs into high gear every October, when American consumers — who spend $13.5 billion annually on Halloween costumes, decorations and candy — look for more haunted tours, attractions and other forms of supernatural exploration. And these fall visitors in search of scares are anything but frightening to tourism boosters, who hope to reverse the 3% dip in downtown hotel occupancy from 2024 to 2025 due to a nationwide drop in international visitors, higher travel costs and a more competitive market for meetings and conventions

“Haunted tourism is a significant part of New Orleans’ visitor economy,” said Alice Glen, an executive at New Orleans & Co., the city's destination marketing organization. "When approached thoughtfully and respectfully, these experiences can deepen historical understanding and build appreciation for the people and places that tell New Orleans’ story."

Vampire movie started an industry

Today's haunted tour companies in New Orleans are carrying on a tradition that started in the 1990s, when industry pioneers like Richard Rochester, founder of Magic Tours, and Sidney Smith, founder of Haunted History Tours, began escorting visitors through the French Quarter and telling stories that captured interest piqued by the local filming of the Tom Cruise movie "Interview with the Vampire" in 1993.

Rochester's initial source material was the book "Ghost Stories of Old New Orleans" by Jeanne deLavigne, according to Randy Bibb, a veteran guide who teaches classes on the topic.

"He was a big, tall guy dressed like a vampire with a loud voice," Bibb said. "When he was putting together the tours, there were no vampire stories, so he had to start making some up — and since he couldn’t create enough of those to satisfy people, he turned to ghosts."

Bibb said some of Rochester's tales, like the story of five boys killed in an 18th-century fire at the current site of the Andrew Jackson Hotel, were created for a practical reason: to fill a blockslong gap between the locations of other existing ghost stories in the Quarter.

Though Rochester himself left town in the early 2000s and Magic Tours is gone, Smith led Haunted History for three decades until his death last year and witnessed the growth of the industry he helped create as TV shows like "Ghost Adventures" reeled in a new generation of thrill seekers.

Rob Florence, a three-decade veteran of the walking tour industry, said when he launched his company, NOLA Historic Tours, in 1995, there were only a handful of other similar businesses in town. Now, there are dozens, including many dedicated to paranormal themes.

A spokesperson for the New Orleans Ground Transportation Bureau, which regulates tour companies, said there are about 900 active tour guide licenses in the city, but that number includes guides of all types. 

"There seems to be a ghost tour on every corner," said Kalila Smith, Sidney Smith's ex-wife and the current operator of the tour company she helped create. "And you can only slice the pie so many ways."

Most nights outside the Lalaurie Mansion at the corner of Royal and Governor Nicholls streets, one of the most famous haunted houses in the country, a half-dozen tour guides compete with each other for volume, outlandishness and theatricality, according to Florence. 

Sometimes, the spectacle leads to controversy.

An unpermitted marketing stunt in July prompted complaints that the "haunted house" treatment of the Lalaurie Mansion is insensitive to the memory of the actual enslaved people who were tortured and killed there in the 1800s.

That incident illustrates a bigger challenge for the industry, according to Nitasha Sharma, an assistant geography professor at the University of Alabama who studies dark tourism.

"The immersive spooky side shouldn't take over the real histories," Sharma said. "People actually suffered at some of the sites where recreational horror is created, so they shouldn't get pushed into the background."

Drew Cantwell, the general manager of The Myrtles Plantation in St. Francisville, said that issue is top of mind at a remote historic home with a reputation for hauntings that's been a tourist attraction since the 1990s.

“We're fully aware and transparent about the terrible things that happened on these grounds year ago," he said. "We encourage guides to tell the history and explain those things, because it’s a great opportunity for learning, and then we also talk about how we're moving forward.”

'Too much going on'

Despite the increase in haunted tour operators and guides in New Orleans, Smith said the business is “not near what it was” when Haunted History debuted more than three decades ago.

She said increased competition combined with declining visitation meant the company's revenue was down 17% year-over-year from 2024 to 2025, and its stable of about 20 guides is half of what it was at its peak.

Jennifer Talley, co-founder of the New Orleans Paranormal Society, which offers "ghost-hunting experiences," blames the downturn she's witnessed on broader trends.

"Tourism in New Orleans has just tanked since 2024," she said. "There's just too much going on and I think everybody is 'New Orleansed out.'"

Susan Weidmann, an assistant professor recreation management at Appalachian State University, said economic challenges aren't just affecting tourism locally.

"Everyone has to cut from their budget, and tourism/recreation and leisure is one of the first things to go," she said. 

Branching out

Not all the tour companies are sitting idle through the slump. 

In July, Talley and her husband, Christopher, hosted their first New Orleans ParaCon, a gathering of psychics, paranormal investigators, UFO experts and more. The event drew several hundred attendees, and she's already working on next year's follow-up.

Black, the former social worker, meanwhile, continues to suit up and hit the street five nights a week, counting on her glowing online reviews to boost business. 

"This work is way more taxing than people realize because, rain or shine, you're outdoors doing tours in the summer heat," she said. "But I love it. I may make less money than I used to, but my mental health is better."

Florence, the tour company owner, said the paranormal tours, like it or not, are a part of the city's landscape.

“It’s fashionable for hip French Quarter people to complain about them," he said. "But that would be like moving to Aspen, Colorado, and complaining about skiing."
